name: Karl Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. What you say is confidential, so feel free to tell me both your public line and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hollow Creek Electric, a rural co-op, which means the farms and villages it serves own it, not shareholders. We've got about four thousand kilometres of line and not many people, so most days I'm on a three-man crew rebuilding old line, out past the grain silos on Route 9, setting new poles and restringing wire. I like the quiet and the long views. What tires me out is the driving, sometimes two hours each way before you even get the outriggers down.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The legs that fold out from the truck so it doesn't tip when the boom goes up. Dwayne, who I've worked with for nineteen years, says I set them like I'm parking a ship. He's probably right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's pretty much what I see now, to be fair. A few handy things and a lot of talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in small doses. I use one of those chat programs now and then to tidy up an incident report, because my spelling's terrible, and it does that fine. I'd tell people not to believe the ads, it's a tool, like a better torque wrench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit relieved. I'm four years off retiring at sixty-two, and I'd like those years to be boring. If nothing radical changes, my plan holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. Keep using the chat thing for paperwork, keep the savings ticking over, we've got about three months put by. Maybe I'd ask the co-op board to spend any money they save on replacing the 1970s line in the east valley, which is a disgrace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a dry, windless day on the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the east valley line a disgrace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The poles are older than my sons and half of them are leaning. Every winter storm we lose a farm or two out there, and old Mrs Haddad goes three days without heat. That's where I'd want any savings to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the co-op would push hardest for AI, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the new general manager, she came from a big city utility. She means well, but she sees the co-op like a business plan. The members elect the board, though, so she can't go too far without them.

S0.say: I'd say AI is useful in small doses, like a better torque wrench. I use it to tidy up my incident reports and I'd tell people not to believe the ads.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, because I'm four years from retiring at sixty-two and I want those years to be boring. If nothing big changes, my plan holds.
S0.do: Keeps working as he is, uses a chat program for paperwork and keeps around three months of savings in place. Asks the co-op board to spend any savings on replacing the old east valley line.
S0.quote: Every winter storm we lose a farm or two out there, and old Mrs Haddad goes three days without heat.
S0.fieldNote: Karl already uses AI lightly and has a balanced, unexcited view of it. His first thought with any saving is the ageing line and the customers who lose heat. He trusts the co-op structure, where members elect the board, to keep management in check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change but time to adjust. I can work with that, as long as we really get the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when the co-op model earns its keep. The members can decide how the change happens, instead of some far-off shareholders. Online I'd say governments should pay for retraining, properly, not with a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly paperwork that changes. Ines, my wife, is a nurse, and she already has AI writing her notes, and she says it saves her half an hour a shift. I think line work stays line work for a good while, because the poles are out in mud and wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let Dwayne's nephew, who's twenty-four and good with computers, show me whatever new tools the co-op brings in, and once I see it working on a couple of jobs I'd use it. I'd join the union's tech committee for a year, since I'm already a member. And I'd keep saving, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a flicker about the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said "once I see it working". What would it have to prove first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it doesn't send us to the wrong pole. We had a mapping system once that put a transformer on the wrong side of the river, and we drove an hour round. Show me it gets the map right ten times and I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linda in dispatch. She takes the outage calls at three in the morning and knows every farm by the owner's first name. A computer could take the calls, sure, but it won't know that the Petersens have a son on oxygen.

S1.say: I'd say this is when the co-op model proves itself, because members decide how change happens. Governments should pay for real retraining, not a leaflet.
S1.think: For me it's mostly the paperwork that changes, the way AI already writes my wife's nursing notes. Line work stays line work for a good while because it happens in mud and wind.
S1.do: Learns new co-op tools from a young colleague once they've proven themselves on a few jobs, and joins the union's tech committee for a year. Keeps saving at the usual rate.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry for the office staff.
S1.quote: A computer could take the calls, sure, but it won't know that the Petersens have a son on oxygen.
S1.fieldNote: Karl's test for any new tool is simple and practical: get the map right ten times. He reads change through his wife's experience as a nurse, which makes him less fearful. His worry goes to the dispatcher, whose local knowledge he sees as the thing a machine would miss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028? That's quick. I'd be sixty, two years before I meant to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in hard, with a safety net for everyone and a tax on the companies making the robots. At work I'd say let's get the union and the co-op board in a room this month. I'd probably post that too, which I don't usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the co-op would be slower than the big companies, because robots are expensive and the members would argue about it. That buys me maybe a year. But two years short of my pension is real money, and three months of savings doesn't go far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Ines that first weekend and work out whether we could live on her wage plus a reduced pension if I went at sixty. We'd stop the plan to redo the kitchen, that's twelve thousand we'd keep. I'd push the union for an early retirement deal, and I'd put everything spare into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but my chest tightens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a robot doing your job actually look like, out on Route 9?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe a truck that sets the pole itself and a drone stringing the wire. I've seen a video of a robot arm doing live-line work from a bucket, and that was already a bit spooky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ines's wage. Is her job safe in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She says nobody's letting a robot put a cannula in her patients, but she said that about the notes too. If her job went as well, then we're in trouble, and I don't have an answer for that. I'd just hope the government had something ready.

S2.say: I'd say governments need to step in hard, with a safety net for everyone and a tax on the robot makers. I'd want the union and the co-op board in a room within the month.
S2.think: I think the co-op would move slower than big companies, which might buy me a year. But being two years short of my pension is real money, and three months of savings won't go far.
S2.do: Works out with his wife in the first weekend whether her wage and a reduced pension could cover them if he leaves at sixty. Cancels the planned twelve-thousand kitchen redo, saves everything spare and pushes the union for an early retirement deal.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest but not panicking.
S2.quote: I've seen a video of a robot arm doing live-line work from a bucket, and that was already a bit spooky.
S2.fieldNote: Karl expects his member-owned co-op to lag behind the market, and that belief steadies him. His plan rests heavily on his wife's nursing job, and when pressed he admits he has no answer if hers goes too. He is candid about not knowing what a robot crew would look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. I'd already be retired by then if all goes to plan. So it's about whether the plan survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to set rules for how robots come in, not argue about whether they will. I'd tell the co-op meeting we should commit to no forced layoffs for older crew. That's a fair ask with five years' notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd likely be fine. I retire at sixty-two in 2030, a year before it lands. My worry is Dwayne, he's fifty-one, and the younger lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and retire at sixty-two as planned. I'd bump our savings by a hundred a month so we've got a bit more when I stop. And I'd spend some evenings with Dwayne's nephew learning whatever drone or robot gear the co-op starts testing, because the crew should have someone old who understands it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more for others than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dwayne, if this were the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get himself onto the robot training first, because he's got fourteen years to go. He'd tell me to mind my own business. Then he'd do it, because he always ends up taking my advice a month later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the crew need someone old who understands it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robot won't know the land. It won't know that the ground by the Okafor creek turns to soup in March and you can't put a truck there. Somebody has to tell it that, at least at first.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years, so let's set the rules for how robots come in instead of arguing about whether they will. I'd ask the co-op to commit to no forced layoffs for older crew.
S3.think: I'd likely be fine because I retire in 2030, a year before it lands. My worry is for Dwayne at fifty-one and the younger lads.
S3.do: Keeps working toward retirement at sixty-two and raises savings by a hundred a month. Spends some evenings learning the drone and robot gear the co-op tests, so the crew has an older hand who understands it.
S3.feel: Uneasy, mostly on behalf of others.
S3.quote: It won't know that the ground by the Okafor creek turns to soup in March and you can't put a truck there.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for Karl's existing retirement plan to clear the landing, and he knows it. He moves from defence to helping others prepare, and he's willing to learn new gear once it's in front of him. His sense of value lies in local knowledge of the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight, hopefully fishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where we have no excuse. Ten years is enough to retrain people and build a fair system, so if we mess it up, it's on the politicians. I'd say it at the co-op annual meeting too, from the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's comfortable, honestly. I'd be retired six years by then. What I think about is my sons, Rafa's a mechanic and he's thirty-two, so he'd be in the middle of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing much changes for me now, I keep working and retire at sixty-two. I'd vote for candidates who back a proper transition fund. And I'd tell Rafa to look at what robots break, because something always breaks, and he's good with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own life, a little uneasy for Rafa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did Rafa say when you've talked about this before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He laughs and says by then he'll be fixing robot trucks instead of diesel ones. He might be right, he's always been quicker than me with new things. I hope he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if it goes wrong it's on the politicians. Not the companies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies will do what companies do, they'll go for cheap. That's why you need the politicians to set the rules. Blaming a company for wanting profit is like blaming the wind for blowing.

S4.say: I'd say ten years leaves no excuse, because it's enough time to retrain people and build a fair system. If it goes wrong, that's on the politicians.
S4.think: For me it's comfortable, since I'd have been retired six years by then. I think about my son Rafa, a mechanic who'd be right in the middle of it.
S4.do: Keeps working and retires at sixty-two as planned. Votes for candidates who back a proper transition fund and encourages his son to look at repairing robots.
S4.feel: Calm about his own life, a little uneasy for his son.
S4.quote: Blaming a company for wanting profit is like blaming the wind for blowing.
S4.fieldNote: Karl puts responsibility squarely on governments to set the rules, rather than on companies. Ten years puts him safely in retirement, so his attention moves to his son. He comes across as steady and practical, with a quiet faith that his son will adapt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it catches me two years short and could catch Ines too. What would help is an early retirement deal for people my age at full pension, paid for partly by the companies selling the robots. And a co-op board that sticks to the members, not to the cheapest option.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the robots. If the co-op owned them, and the savings went back to the members as cheaper power, I'd feel very different. If some big firm just rented them to us, I'd feel robbed. Ownership is the whole thing, really.

headlineQuote: If the co-op owned them, and the savings went back to the members as cheaper power, I'd feel very different.
portrait: Karl Moreau is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker who rebuilds old line for Hollow Creek Electric, a member-owned rural co-op, alongside his partner of nineteen years, Dwayne. He uses AI now and then for paperwork and is open to new tools once they prove themselves on the job. The hype and slow-change pictures barely touch him, and he trusts the co-op to move carefully. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious because it lands two years before his pension and could hit his wife's nursing job too. With five or ten years he relaxes into his plan to retire at sixty-two and turns his worry towards his colleague and his son.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would catch him two years short of retirement and might affect his wife's job too.
whatWouldHelp: An early retirement deal at full pension for people his age, partly paid for by the robot companies, and a co-op board that stays loyal to its members.
